The respective numbers of choices are 3,2,1,2,2,2,3,3, whose product is 432. This uses exactly the stated divisor restrictions, without imposing a condition involving the unpainted integer 1.

routes.label: Equal distances and midpoint area halves

audits.mathematicalReason: The angle-bisector theorem gives BG:GC = 50:10 = 5:1, so triangle ABG has area 100. Since DE is a midsegment parallel to BC, triangle ADF is similar to ABG with scale factor 1/2 and area 25. Quadrilateral FDBG is ABG minus ADF, so its area is 75. The alternative route is also valid: equal distances from the bisector to AB and AC give the same 5:1 area ratios, while successive midpoint area halves give area ADE = 30 and area ADF = 25. The two routes need not be combined.

The triangle's altitude to its side of length 24 is √(15²-12²) = 9, so its area is 108 and semiperimeter is 27. Its inradius is therefore 4. Let H be the perpendicular projection of O onto the triangle's plane. At a tangency point T, the right triangle OHT gives HT² + OH² = 36, so H is equidistant from the three side lines and the section circle has radius 4. Consequently OH = √(36-16) = 2√5. Even if tangency were interpreted using supporting lines, the exradii 9,9,36 exceed 6 and are impossible. Both variants are defensible; Heron's formula is an alternative to the altitude-area computation.

routes.label: Reduce to a linear logarithmic equation
Obtain a quadratic in the inner logarithm

audits.mathematicalReason: The nested logarithms require n > 1. Set t = log_16(n) > 0, so log_4(n) = 2t. The equation becomes log_2(t) = (1+log_2(t))/2, giving log_2(t) = 1 and t = 2. Thus n = 16² = 256, whose digit sum is 13. Alternatively, exponentiating in base 4 gives t² = 2t; the domain excludes t = 0 and leaves t = 2. Both routes respect the logarithmic domain.

The diagonals share midpoint (0,0) and have equal lengths, so PQRS is a rectangle. Its adjacent side lengths are √2(a-b) and √2(a+b), giving area 2(a-b)(a+b) = 16. Shoelace independently gives the same area 2(a²-b²). Put d = a-b and s = a+b. Then ds = 8, s > d > 0, and d,s have the same parity. Of the ordered factor pairs (1,8) and (2,4), only (2,4) has matching parity. Hence a = 3, b = 1, and a+b = 4.

The right side is 5/12 - 4/12 = 1/12. Adding 3/4 to both sides gives x = 1/12 + 9/12 = 5/6. Alternatively, multiplying the original equation by 12 gives 12x-9 = 5-4 and hence the same solution. The simple-equation assessment and both supporting routes fit.

Let the team total be T. Integer scores T/4 and 2T/7 force T = 28k for a positive integer k. After Alexa and Brittany, the remaining score is (1-1/4-2/7)T = 13k. If R is the seven other players' combined score, then R = 13k-15 and 0 ≤ R ≤ 14. Thus 15 ≤ 13k ≤ 29, forcing k = 2 and R = 11. This total is feasible with seven nonnegative integer scores at most 2, so the finite integer restriction is complete.

Each round has 12 equally likely ordered donor-recipient pairs, so there are 12⁴ equally likely transfer sequences. Returning all holdings to four coins means equal incoming and outgoing transfers at every player. A balanced four-edge directed multigraph consists either of a directed four-cycle or of two directed two-cycles. Four-cycles contribute 6·4! = 144 sequences. Repeating one two-cycle contributes 6·4!/(2!2!) = 36. Choosing two distinct two-cycles contributes C(6,2)·4! = 360. Thus the probability is 540/12⁴ = 5/192. A recurrence retaining the four net coin changes is also valid. Starting with four coins ensures no transfer is blocked during these four rounds.

Choose D=(0,0), C=(1,0), A=(0,1), B=(1,1), and write Q_i=(q_i,0). Intersecting AQ_i with BD gives P_i=(q_i/(1+q_i), q_i/(1+q_i)), hence q_(i+1)=q_i/(1+q_i). Similar triangles give the same recurrence. Since q_1=1/2, reciprocals satisfy 1/q_(i+1)=1/q_i+1, so q_i=1/(i+1). The ith area is q_i q_(i+1)/2 = (q_i-q_(i+1))/2. Therefore the first N areas sum to 1/4 - 1/[2(N+2)], which tends to 1/4. This explicitly verifies the vanishing endpoint after finite telescoping rather than assuming convergence from cancellation alone.
